newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Swedish bank merger flurry seen continuing.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Swedish bank merger flurry seen continuing.

text.p: A merger flurry in the Swedish banking sector continued on Tuesday and analysts forecast more reshuffling at home before banks cast their eyes overseas for foreign brides.
Swedbank and Foreningsbanken announced that they would merge, creating the country's second largest bank with a large retail customer base and strong rural presence.
The move follows Handelsbanken's acquisition of mortgage lender Stadshypotek, which was finalised on Monday and created the largest bank in Sweden.
"The deal between Swedbank and Foreningsbanken adds pressure on Nordbanken and S-E-Banken to resume talks," Matthew Czepliewicz, analyst with Salomon Brothers, said.
"Swedish banks, first of all Handelsbanken, are likely to seriously start looking abroad in 1998."
Nordbanken and S-E-Banken said two weeks ago that merger talks had failed. But analysts say they are likely to do something soon.

S-E-Banken has been involved in merger talks with both Handelsbanken and Nordbanken and is generally seen eager to find a partner as it will lose a large part of its important foreign exchange income if European economic and monetary union (EMU) starts on January 1, 1999.
And the government has said it intends to sell its 58 percent Nordbanken stake.
"If they do not merge, Nordbanken could buy back more of the state's stake and S-E-Banken could merge with an insurance company in Sweden or Finland," an analyst in Copenhagen said.
"A bank and an insurance company will have a huge customer basis and a large potential for cross selling. In addition, some overheads could be cut."
He did not, however, see a rush of cross-border mergers just yet.

"In three to five years, when the single currency is introduced, banks will realise how much income they will lose, how much the new technology will cost and how strong competition from abroad will be. Then we will see cross-border mergers," he said.
A London analyst agreed, saying: "Swedish banks need to make themselves strong on their home market before starting to look elsewhere."
But when the time for foreign expansion comes, Czepliewicz expected Handelsbanken to be the first one out of the traps.
"While S-E-Banken has opened some branches abroad, Handelsbanken has a stronger position for foreign expansion as it is better capitalised and larger," Czepliewicz said.

Analysts did not see much risk of Swedish banks becoming easy prey for foreign takeovers while concentrating on domestic operations. On the contrary, their domestic strength should shield them from hostile advances, they said.
"The stronger your position in the household sector, the middle market and the small company market, the less attractive you are for foreign banks," Czepliewicz said.
But S-E-Banken, which is active at the top corporate level could be more vulnerable, he said.
The Copenhagen analyst said, however, that a foreign bank interested in having a strong presence in Sweden might go for Nordbanken as it is so large and profitable.
